questions.question_stem: A group of organizations needs a shared record of events, but no single organization is trusted to run the master database. What core problem is a blockchain meant to address in this situation?
questions.correct_answer: It lets distributed participants agree on a shared history by applying common rules without a central referee.
incorrect_answers: It encrypts every shared record for members and regulators, guaranteeing private ledger access to every party by default.
It replaces independent servers with one managed cloud ledger that instantly copies all large files to peers on request.
It creates a central permission list so one appointed administrator decides which firms may view shared ledgers.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames blockchain as an append-only state machine for maintaining shared reality among distributed participants without relying on one central authority.

questions.question_stem: A node receives a transaction claiming to spend Alice's funds. Which blockchain pillar is most directly responsible for proving Alice authorized that transaction without revealing her private key?
questions.correct_answer: Cryptography, through digital signatures that can be verified by the network.
incorrect_answers: Peer networking, through gossip messages that relay signed data among many nodes.
Consensus rules, through miner voting that decides Alice meant to spend funds.
Access controls, through a central database that validates Alice's login token.
questions.explanation: Digital signatures are the lesson's authorization mechanism: they let nodes verify intent without needing a password server or exposure of the private key.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/introduction_02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance-slides-only.qmd: Pillar 1: Cryptography; Step 1: Creation and Signing

questions.question_stem: Two validators each assemble a different valid-looking next block at about the same time. Which part of the blockchain architecture is meant to resolve which block becomes the official next step in the chain?
questions.correct_answer: The consensus mechanism, because it provides rules for selecting the accepted next block.
incorrect_answers: The mempool service, because it permanently ranks unconfirmed payments for validators.
The user's wallet, because it chooses the cryptographic layout of incoming blocks.
The hash pointers, because they alone pick one candidate block from valid rivals.
questions.explanation: Consensus is the rule system that lets nodes converge on the official next block when multiple candidate blocks or conflicts exist.

questions.question_stem: A transaction has been broadcast and relayed by several nodes, but it has not yet appeared in a block. What is the best interpretation of its status?
questions.correct_answer: It is valid enough to be pending in the mempool, but it is not finalized on the chain yet.
incorrect_answers: It is fully confirmed because relay gossip already counts as final network agreement.
It was deleted because nodes never keep valid transactions before block inclusion.
It skipped consensus because mempool entries write directly to the shared ledger.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes network awareness from finality: valid broadcast transactions wait in the mempool until selected for a block and accepted through consensus.
questions.lesson_block: Putting it Together: The Lifecycle of a Transaction

questions.question_stem: Which sequence best matches the lesson's transaction lifecycle from user intent to shared ledger update?
questions.correct_answer: Sign the transaction, broadcast it to nodes, wait pending in the mempool, include it in a candidate block, reach consensus, then append the block.
incorrect_answers: Broadcast the transaction first, append it to a local chain immediately, sign it after inclusion, then ask consensus to validate the sender.
Sign the transaction, store it as a private wallet note, let the recipient adjust balances directly, then publish a summary to validators afterward.
Send it to the recipient, let that recipient choose a miner, add it to a finalized block, then broadcast the signed payment to peer nodes.
questions.explanation: The lesson's flow moves from creation and signing to P2P broadcast, pending mempool status, block assembly, consensus, and hash-linked block addition.

questions.question_stem: An attacker changes a transaction in an old block. Why does the lesson say this disrupts the chain rather than remaining a hidden edit?
questions.correct_answer: Changing the old block changes its hash, which breaks the hash link expected by later blocks.
incorrect_answers: Changing the old block exposes the attacker's private key to every validating network node and wallet.
Changing the old block makes all later transactions anonymous across the whole public network.
Changing the old block clears the mempool, stopping nodes from receiving new pending payments.
questions.explanation: Hash links make the ledger tamper-evident: if earlier data changes, its digital fingerprint changes, so later blocks no longer point cleanly to the expected prior block.

questions.question_stem: A startup proposes storing high-resolution video files directly on a public blockchain so the files are replicated forever. What is the strongest lesson-grounded critique?
questions.correct_answer: Blockchains are designed for expensive, append-only state transitions and receipts, not cheap bulk file storage.
incorrect_answers: Blockchains cannot store user data because blocks contain only peer network addresses and routing hints.
Public chains work well only when every validating node is a licensed institution with known operators.
Consensus rules stop databases from copying transaction histories onto more than one machine at a time during audits.
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly warns against treating blockchains as distributed cloud drives; on-chain space is expensive and suited to state changes, not large media files.
questions.lesson_block: Common Misconceptions: What a Blockchain is NOT

questions.question_stem: A user says their public blockchain activity is completely anonymous because their wallet address is not their legal name. What correction best matches the lesson?
questions.correct_answer: Public chain activity is pseudonymous; if the address is linked to the person, its public history can become traceable.
incorrect_answers: Public chain activity is fully private; validator encryption prevents outsiders from reading ledger entries.
Public chain activity is anonymous; mempool relay strips identity before a block confirms each transfer fully.
Public chain records become untraceable because consensus deletes earlier address history from all full nodes.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes anonymity from pseudonymity: addresses may not start with real names, but transaction histories are public and linkable if identity is later attached.
questions.lesson_block: Common Misconceptions: What a Blockchain is NOT

questions.question_stem: A consortium of banks wants a shared ledger among known participants, with stronger privacy controls and higher performance than an open public network. Which model fits the lesson's tradeoff discussion best?
questions.correct_answer: A permissioned blockchain, because participation can be restricted to approved institutions.
incorrect_answers: A permissionless blockchain, because it limits validators to approved anonymous miners.
A public mempool system, because it removes the need for shared consensus rules outright.
A centralized cloud database, because it keeps decentralization without any governing network.
questions.explanation: The lesson presents permissioned chains as better aligned with known-participant settings where privacy, institutional controls, and performance matter more than open participation.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/introduction_02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance-slides-only.qmd: Permissionless vs. Permissioned Ledgers; Spectrum of Decentralization

questions.question_stem: A team claims that because blockchain signatures and hashes are strong, users cannot lose assets to attacks. Which lesson-grounded response is most accurate?
questions.correct_answer: Strong core cryptography does not eliminate endpoint risks such as wallet compromise, phishing, exchanges, or smart contract bugs.
incorrect_answers: Strong cryptography makes wallet apps and exchange accounts immune to operational security failures across all user devices by default.
Hashing fixes user mistakes by automatically reversing fraudulent blockchain transfers after miner review and approval.
Consensus rules let honest nodes recover stolen private keys for users after a reported endpoint attack by wallet support.
questions.explanation: The lesson separates the strength of cryptographic primitives from the vulnerability of endpoints and user-facing systems.
questions.lesson_block: Common Misconceptions: What a Blockchain is NOT

questions.question_stem: Alice's Bitcoin wallet selects one prior unspent output worth more than her purchase. Why might the resulting transaction include an output back to Alice?
questions.correct_answer: Bitcoin inputs are spent whole, so the wallet creates a change output for leftover value not paid to Bob or used as a fee.
incorrect_answers: Bitcoin requires each transaction to pay the sender twice to prove control of the signing key before network relay.
Change outputs are miner rewards that replace ordinary fees when a transaction is relayed to block producers and validators.
The P2P network adds a refund output automatically while gossiping the transaction to validating nodes and wallet clients.
questions.explanation: The reading explains the UTXO model: transactions consume previous outputs and create new outputs, often including ordinary change outputs because inputs are indivisible.
questions.specific_source_reading: /tmp/reading-02-ch02.adoc: Transaction Inputs and Outputs; Making Change; Coin Selection

questions.question_stem: A simplified Bitcoin transaction consumes inputs totaling 1.00 BTC and creates outputs totaling 0.995 BTC. According to the reading, what happens to the remaining 0.005 BTC?
questions.correct_answer: It is the implied transaction fee available to the miner who includes the transaction in a valid block.
incorrect_answers: It is burned because Bitcoin forbids leftover value from remaining after outputs are made by wallets.
It becomes an explicit output that wallets must add for the current block producer to claim after mining.
It stays in the original input because UTXOs can be partly consumed by design during spending.
questions.explanation: The reading states that transaction fees are implicit: the fee is the difference between total input value and total output value, not a separate required output.
questions.specific_source_reading: /tmp/reading-02-ch02.adoc: Transaction Inputs and Outputs; Creating the Outputs

questions.question_stem: Bob sees Alice's Bitcoin transaction reach the network within seconds. Why does the reading say waiting for additional confirmations gives Bob stronger settlement confidence?
questions.correct_answer: Each later block built on top of the transaction's block adds proof of work an attacker would need to replace.
incorrect_answers: Each later block encrypts Alice's payment data until public nodes can no longer read it afterward, even for auditors.
Each later block sends Bob a new private key so he can reverse unauthorized payments if needed later.
Each later block erases the transaction from full nodes except the miner who produced its block record.
questions.explanation: The reading treats confirmations as accumulated proof-of-work security: reversal becomes increasingly costly as more blocks build on top of the block containing the transaction.
